name: Primary Lymphedema

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical diagnostic criteria for primary lymphedema

criteria.description: Persistent, non-pitting swelling of one or more limbs lasting more than 3 months
Exclusion of secondary causes of lymphedema such as infection, malignancy, or trauma
Positive family history of lymphedema or hereditary lymphatic abnormalities
Imaging evidence of lymphatic hypoplasia or aplasia on lymphoscintigraphy
Onset of swelling typically before age 40 (congenital or praecox forms)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Persistent limb swelling >3 months with exclusion of secondary causes and supportive imaging findings
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is clinical supported by imaging; genetic testing may assist in some cases.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Chronic non-pitting edema of the lower limb
pathognomonic.notes: Typically unilateral but can be bilateral

pathognomonic.symptomName: Stemmer sign (inability to pinch skin at base of second toe)

common.symptomName: Skin thickening and fibrosis over affected limb
searchTerms: skin thickening and hardening over limb
fibrotic skin changes on affected limb

common.symptomName: Heaviness or tightness sensation in affected limb
searchTerms: tight sensation in arm or leg

common.symptomName: Recurrent cellulitis or erysipelas in affected limb

searchTerms: thickened rough skin with wart-like bumps
skin with excess keratin and papillomas

occasional.symptomName: Lymphangiectasia (dilated lymphatic vessels visible on skin)
Pain or discomfort localized to affected limb
searchTerms: aching in affected arm or leg

occasional.symptomName: Limited range of motion in affected joints

rare.symptomName: Lymphorrhea (leakage of lymph fluid through skin)

searchTerms: milky fluid in chest or abdomen

laboratory: Normal routine blood tests; inflammatory markers elevated during cellulitis episodes
imaging: Lymphoscintigraphy showing lymphatic hypoplasia or aplasia
Ultrasound demonstrating dermal thickening and absence of normal lymphatic channels
genetic: Mutations in FLT4 (VEGFR3), FOXC2, or other lymphatic development genes in some familial cases
other: Positive Stemmer sign on physical examination

distinguishingFeatures: History of malignancy, surgery, infection or trauma causing lymphatic obstruction
Onset usually after an inciting event
Symmetric lower limb fat deposition sparing feet
Pain and tenderness common, no Stemmer sign
Presence of varicose veins, venous stasis changes
Pitting edema more common, improves with leg elevation

redFlags: Unilateral swelling with associated pain and erythema suggesting infection
Presence of systemic symptoms such as fever or weight loss
references: Rockson SG. Lymphedema. Am J Med. 2001 Nov;111(7): 468-72.
International Society of Lymphology. The diagnosis and treatment of peripheral lymphedema: 2020 Consensus Document.
